title: The Pitching Coach Mirage
subtitle: Per-coach FIP outcomes on acquired pitchers span 3.7 runs across 33 coaches — a range that screams hidden signal. After an honest partial-pooling test, 32 of 33 coaches' effects collapse into noise. Reputation does not survive the math.

sections.content: When veteran scouts talk about why a pitcher's ERA improved post-trade, they almost always reach for the same explanation: the new pitching coach. Particular names — Oscar Marin, Roger McDowell, Mark Prior, Dave Eiland — get a reputation as fixers. Others — Mel Stottlemyre Jr., Curt Young, Mike Maddux — get reputations as breakers. The published GM Edge Decomposition on this site identified "org dev fit" as one of the strongest predictors of acquired-pitcher outcomes. The natural next question is whether that signal lives in the pitching coach's identity specifically. The answer is no, and the way the answer arrives is the more interesting part.

The first chart is the deceptive one. Sort all 33 coaches by their raw mean FIP delta on acquired pitchers — the change in fielding-independent pitching from the season before the trade to the season after. The range is 3.67 runs. That is enormous. If it were real, it would be the single most exploitable personnel signal in the trade market.

sections.title: Raw mean FIP delta on acquired pitchers, by pitching coach (n ≥ 10)
sections.y_label: Mean FIP delta (negative = acquired pitchers improved)
sections.caption: Each bar is one pitching coach's mean FIP change on the pitchers their team acquired during their tenure (2010–2024, n ≥ 10). Orange bars = acquired pitchers worsened on FIP. Blue bars = acquired pitchers improved. Range is 3.7 runs. Looks like obvious signal.

sections.title: Why the raw means are not the answer
sections.content: The smallest sample in this chart is n = 10 acquired pitchers; the largest is n = 34. The within-coach standard deviation of FIP delta runs from 1.0 to over 7.0. With that much noise on samples this small, the standard error on each coach's mean can easily reach ±1.0 run on its own — comparable to the gaps between coaches in the chart. The visual range is mostly the chart conflating real differences with sampling noise from short tenures and high-variance outcomes.

The honest test is partial pooling. A Bayesian hierarchical model treats each coach's true effect as a draw from a league-wide distribution. Coaches with small samples get shrunk hard toward the league mean — because their raw mean is mostly noise. Coaches with large samples and consistent outcomes shrink less. The amount of shrinkage is determined by the data itself, not chosen by the analyst. The result is a per-coach posterior with a 90% credible interval that honestly accounts for what we do and don't know.

The forest plot below shows each coach's post-pooling posterior mean and 90% CI. Same coaches, same order, same y-axis as before. The story is different.

sections.title: Partial-pooled posterior mean (orange dot) with 90% credible interval (whiskers)
sections.x_label: Posterior mean FIP delta on acquired pitchers
sections.caption: Each row is one coach. Orange dot = posterior mean. Whiskers = 90% credible interval. Dashed reference line at zero. Almost every coach's interval crosses zero — meaning we cannot credibly distinguish their effect from the league average. Only Mel Stottlemyre Jr. survives the test, and not in the direction the scout-room narrative would predict.

sections.title: The reveal
sections.content: Of the 33 pitching coaches with enough sample to enter the model, exactly one has a 90% credible interval that excludes zero: Mel Stottlemyre Jr., at +0.38 [+0.04, +1.06]. The remaining 32 — including every fixer-archetype name at the top of the raw chart — collapse to posteriors centered near the league mean with intervals that span both directions. The hierarchical model is telling us, quietly: the variation in raw means is what variation in raw means usually is at this sample size — noise.

The shrinkage scatter below makes the mechanism visible. Each dot is one coach: x-axis is their raw mean FIP delta (the deceptive view), y-axis is their pooled posterior mean (the honest view). The further a coach starts from zero on x, the more they get pulled back toward zero on y. The further-out raw means do not get respected by the model because they're attached to small samples. The result is a near-flat band of pooled posteriors regardless of where the raw mean was.

sections.title: Raw vs partial-pooled per-coach FIP delta (each dot is a coach, sized by n)
sections.caption: Coaches whose raw mean is far from zero get aggressively shrunk toward zero in the pooled posterior — exactly because the raw extreme value was probably a small-sample fluke. The pooled-posterior y-values cluster in a tight band around the league mean. The shrinkage is the model honestly admitting how much of the raw range was noise.

sections.content:
A natural rebuttal: maybe the effect lives one level higher. Maybe the pitching coach is the wrong unit of analysis and the receiving organization as a whole is the unit that matters. The same partial-pooling model run at the team level produces a strikingly different result.

Four of twenty-nine teams have post-pooling 90% credible intervals that exclude zero on acquired-pitcher FIP delta. The signal is asymmetric and probably uncomfortable for some readers: every credibly-different org is on the negative-for-the-pitcher side. Colorado, the Cubs, Miami, and Minnesota credibly *worsen* the FIP of pitchers they acquire. No team in the dataset can be credibly distinguished as making acquired pitchers better. The org-level signal exists; it points to environments to avoid as a pitcher rather than orgs that fix you.

sections.title: Same partial-pooled model at the org level (n ≥ 10 pitcher acquisitions per org)
sections.x_label: Posterior mean FIP delta on acquired pitchers
sections.caption: Same Bayesian partial-pooling model, applied to acquiring organizations instead of pitching coaches. Four orgs — COL, CHC, MIA, MIN — have 90% CIs above zero, meaning they credibly worsen the FIP of acquired pitchers. No org's CI sits below zero. The 'this org fixes pitchers' archetype does not survive the test; the 'this org is bad for pitchers' archetype does.

sections.title: Two findings, one inference
sections.content: Pitching coach identity: 1 of 33 credible. Organization identity: 4 of 29 credible. The 'org dev fit' signal from the GM Edge Decomposition piece does exist at the team level, but it is not located in the pitching coach's name. The structure has to live elsewhere in the org — front-office pitching infrastructure, pitching strategy department, biomechanics labs, scouting-to-coaching information flow. The coach is the visible face of an effect whose causal source is upstream.

There is a temptation to read this article as a defense of analytics over scouts. It is not. The scout-room intuition that some pitching coaches are better than others may still be correct in a deeper sense — coaches may differentially help individual pitchers in ways that average out across heterogeneous arms, or the value they add may be visible in metrics this analysis does not use (pitch movement gains, velocity preservation, injury avoidance). What the article rules out is the simplest reading: that the per-coach FIP delta is interpretable on its own. It is not. The raw bar chart at the top of this page should not be used to grade a coach, even informally.

The more useful inference is upstream. The GM Edge Decomposition found that org-level dev fit predicts acquired-pitcher outcomes. This article shows that the pitching coach is not the mechanism — at least not the dominant one. The next question is what is. Pitching strategist roles, bullpen catchers with biomechanics responsibilities, integrated video review, pre-acquisition medical screening — none of these are public data the way coaching staffs are. The signal exists. The visible person is not its source.

stats.label: Orgs credible after pooling
stats.subtext: all credibly bad for acquired pitchers

methodology_note: Per-pitching-coach data: 631 acquired-pitcher trade-legs from 2010–2024, joined from the V3 combined feature/outcome matrix to the `coaches` table (job_code = COAP, 'Pitching Coach'), keyed by (team_id, season). Coach assigned per (receiver_team, trade_season) — the first listed pitching coach per season when multiple are credited. Sample restricted to coaches with at least 10 acquired pitchers (33 coaches). Bayesian hierarchical model: y_i ~ Normal(μ + α_coach[i], σ); α_coach ~ Normal(0, τ); μ ~ Normal(0, 1), τ ~ HalfNormal(0.4), σ ~ HalfNormal(3). Fit in PyMC, 2 chains × 1,500 draws after 1,500 tune, target_accept = 0.95. Posterior means and 90% credible intervals reported. The same model is run on the org-level data (n = 29 orgs with ≥10 acquired pitchers). Both models use identical priors and were checked for convergence (some ESS warnings on the coach model — small sample sizes mean some α_coach posteriors are wide, which is the point of the article).
